A Luxury Honeymoon in Egypt: The Nile and the Sea for Two

How to plan a luxury Egypt honeymoon: the best months, which boat to choose, the Red Sea to finish, a sample twelve days and what it costs

25 November 2026 · 14 minute read

By Islam Hussein, Sillage Égypte journey designer. Last updated: November 2026.

The quick answer

Yes, Egypt makes a fine luxury honeymoon when it is paced for two: temples in the early morning, the river through the afternoon, and the Red Sea to finish. For romance on the river, choose The Complete Egypt, with five nights on a private dahabiya. For the river and the beach, choose The Nile & the Red Sea. Ten to twelve days is the right length, October to April the kindest window, and the final third of the journey should have no alarm clock at all.

A luxury honeymoon in Egypt usually begins as one partner's idea. The wish we hear most goes: one of us wants the pyramids, the other wants a week of doing nothing by the sea: can one journey hold both without wearing us out? It can, and it has less to do with money than with shape. This post covers the months worth marrying around, the rhythm that keeps a honeymoon from becoming a tour, the rooms worth asking for, and a sample twelve days with its price. Sillage Égypte (sillage-egypte.com) is the private Egypt journey designer: every journey private throughout, your own car and your own certified Egyptologist from the first day to the last. A honeymoon is the one journey where that privacy is the entire point.

The short answer: is Egypt good for a luxury honeymoon?

Yes, if it is paced like a honeymoon rather than a tour: monuments in the cool of the morning, the river through the afternoon, the sea at the end. Egypt suits this unusually well. Its halves are opposites (one of the world's densest monumental landscapes, then several hundred kilometres of warm, quiet coast), so the change of pace is built into the country rather than engineered around it. And its crowds are a clock problem, which is to say a solvable one: the Valley of the Kings opens at 06:00, and the early hour is the quiet one.

Two honest qualifications: this is not a resort fortnight (the middle week includes 05:00 starts, and the month matters more than the thread count), and Egypt is simply the wrong answer for some couples, worth knowing before the flights.

Who it suits, and who should marry elsewhere

The shape suits couples who want a country worth talking about for the next thirty years, and who share early mornings well enough; autumn and spring weddings fit it almost perfectly. It does not suit a honeymoon whose dream is pure stillness, no plans and no wake-up calls: that couple should take the Red Sea alone. And it does not suit a week: with eight days or fewer, or while jet lag still has you, choose two of the three Egypts rather than all of them at a run. We say so plainly when it applies, as in why we sometimes talk you out of a trip.

The best months for an Egypt honeymoon

October to April is the window, and the two sweet spots within it are late October to early December and late February to early April: warm, clear, neither peak-crowded nor peak-priced. In winter proper, Cairo reaches 19 to 21 °C by day and Luxor and Aswan 23 to 26 °C, with nights of about 7 to 12 °C. The Red Sea stays swimmable all year, at about 21 to 23 °C in winter and about 29 °C in August, and still about 27 °C in October, so autumn honeymoons get the sea at its best just as the valley cools.

Months Cairo and the valley The Red Sea Crowds and rates
October to November Cairo about 30 °C falling to 25 °C; Upper Egypt hotter in October (Aswan about 36 °C) Around 26 to 27 °C Moderate
December to early January The finest light; 19 to 26 °C by day About 23 °C Peak: book 9 to 12 months ahead
January to February Cool mornings, quieter sites About 21 to 23 °C The quietest months
March to early April Cairo 24 to 28 °C; Luxor and Aswan 30 °C and above From about 22 °C, warming Moderate
May to September Luxor and Aswan about 41 °C by day in June to August 27 to 29 °C, the warmest sea Empty monuments; the heat is the price

Figures are typical, not forecasts. Three dates to plan around:

  • The festive fortnight, roughly 20 December to 5 January, is Egypt's best weather and biggest crowds arriving together. It is a wonderful honeymoon window if, and only if, it is booked far ahead; the best boats and suites go nine to twelve months out. Our Christmas and New Year in Egypt guide covers the detail.
  • June to August is genuinely hot: Luxor and Aswan average about 41 °C by day. Marry in June, and our honest counsel is to delay the journey to October, or keep to the sea and Cairo's museums, and save the temples for a second journey together.
  • 22 February and 22 October at Abu Simbel, the rising sun travels the temple's axis into the inner sanctuary and lights the statue of Ramesses II, then those of Amun and Ra-Horakhty, while Ptah's stays in shadow. It is famous, and the surrounding days are quieter and just as warm. In 2027, 22 February falls during Ramadan.

The whole year is compared in when to go to Egypt.

The shape of the trip: temples in the morning, the river in the afternoon, the sea to finish

The shape that works is a rhythm rather than a checklist: Cairo first, while jet lag makes early starts easy; the river through the middle week, as the celebrating catches up with you; the sea at the end, when nothing should be timed.

Cairo and Giza, two or three nights. The plateau in the first hour, Saqqara before lunch, the Grand Egyptian Museum on a slow afternoon: a walking pace, not a checkpoint pace. Jet lag is a scheduling asset in Egypt; you would be awake at five anyway.

The river, four or five nights. This is the middle week's hotel, and there are two ways to take it, set out below.

Abu Simbel as an overnight, if you add it. On Sillage journeys Abu Simbel is always reached by air. Fly down from Aswan and you have the temples in late light, after the day-trippers have flown back, and a quiet night beside Lake Nasser.

The sea, four nights. The Oberoi Sahl Hasheesh, an all-suite resort south of Hurghada, and days in which the only decision is whether to swim before or after lunch: the half most itineraries forget.

Notes from our Egyptologists

  • Stone before ten, water after noon. The valley's sites are coolest, emptiest and best-lit in the first two hours; every serious plan is built around this rule.
  • The Valley of the Kings opens at 06:00. Tombs close from time to time for conservation, so which three to enter is a decision your Egyptologist makes that morning, not on the flight over.
  • Deir el-Medina, the village of the men who cut the royal tombs, is the site couples remember longest: small, painted, full of the everyday life the great temples never mention.
  • At Edfu, arrive early. The Temple of Horus is one of the best-preserved temples in Egypt, and its colonnades repay silence.
  • Kom Ombo, the double temple of Sobek and Horus, stands right above the river, so it is an easy stop from the boat.

The boat question: the decision that most changes a honeymoon

The single decision that most changes an Egypt honeymoon is the boat, and it decides which journey you want.

A private dahabiya, on The Complete Egypt. A dahabiya is a shallow-draught traditional Nile sailing boat, typically with 8 to 12 cabins, air-conditioned and en suite. On The Complete Egypt it is yours for five nights from Esna to Aswan, sailing upstream on the north wind, with all meals aboard. On a honeymoon the difference is less luxury than geography: a dahabiya's shallow draught lets it moor at Gebel el-Silsila, El-Kab and other quiet anchorages. This is the most romantic thing Egypt offers, and the journey has no beach at the end.

The Oberoi Zahra, on The Nile & the Red Sea. A luxury cruiser of 27 to 28 cabins and suites, for four nights from Aswan to Luxor, with Seti I and Ramesses VI tickets included. You share the ship with its other guests, while your car and your Egyptologist stay yours. In return you get the road from Luxor to the sea at the end.

Want a dahabiya and the sea in one journey? Ask. It can be designed, and the routing is set out in your proposal.

Where to stay: the rooms worth asking for

Spend your attention on the view, and keep the rest simple. Egypt's historic hotels are part of the pleasure. The Marriott Mena House at Giza has taken guests since 1886 and sits at the foot of the pyramids; its historic Palace Wing is reported closed long-term, and Pyramid-view rooms are sold in the garden wing. The former Old Cataract in Aswan, opened in January 1900 and now the Mandarin Oriental, has its Palace Wing open while the Nile Wing is renovated to July 2027. The Winter Palace in Luxor, opened in 1907, is closed for restoration and reported to reopen in July 2027, so your Luxor hotel, where you need one, is named in your proposal.

These are independent houses, not ours, and any can be swapped to suit. Tell us whether you want a Pyramid or Nile view, and your proposal names the hotels and the room we have requested for each night. A room type is requested, not promised.

On the coast, the Oberoi Sahl Hasheesh does the job a honeymoon wants from the sea: suites, water and quiet, not a programme.

A sample twelve-day itinerary

One shape we can plan, on the route of The Nile & the Red Sea and ending by the sea, written out so the rhythm is visible. Days can be trimmed or stretched; this is a starting point, not a fixed programme, and the order of the river days follows the ship's sailing.

  1. Cairo, arrival. Met inside the terminal, Egyptian entry visa arranged in advance; the drive to your hotel; sleep.
  2. Giza and Saqqara. The plateau in the first hour, on foot; Saqqara's step pyramid before lunch. (The Empty Plateau, two hours opened for your party alone, is subject to official permission for the date: it is requested on booking, and the permission and its cost are confirmed in writing before the balance is due.)
  3. Cairo, slowly. Coptic and Islamic Cairo, or the Grand Egyptian Museum; the last city night.
  4. Fly to Aswan. Board the Oberoi Zahra.
  5. Aswan. Philae by boat; the first evening on the river.
  6. Kom Ombo and Edfu. The temples early, the afternoon on deck as the ship sails north.
  7. Luxor. The west bank at 06:00: the Valley of the Kings with Seti I and Ramesses VI, then Deir el-Medina and the terraces of Hatshepsut; Karnak at the soft end of the afternoon.
  8. To the sea. Off the ship and by road from Luxor to the Oberoi Sahl Hasheesh, four to five hours.
  9. Nothing timed. The sea in the morning; sleep in the afternoon.
  10. Nothing timed. The same again, on purpose.
  11. Nothing timed. A last long day by the water.
  12. Home. The flight from Hurghada to Cairo, and your flight home.

One day on the dahabiya, hour by hour

If you choose the dahabiya on The Complete Egypt, a day runs like this, the whole rhythm in miniature:

  • 05:45: tea on deck; the river grey-blue and empty in first light.
  • 06:30: breakfast for two; the crew cast off.
  • 07:30: the Temple of Horus at Edfu, still quiet.
  • 10:00: back aboard; the day's sightseeing is done.
  • 12:30: lunch as the bank slides by.
  • 15:00: the deck, a book, a nap; sailing when the wind is fair.
  • 16:45: tea; the quarries of Gebel el-Silsila appear on the bank.
  • 18:00: moored at the quarry anchorage; the light goes long.
  • 20:00: dinner on deck.
  • 22:00: asleep by ten, most nights.

Trim days 3 and 11 for a ten-day journey, or add a night at Abu Simbel, by air, for a fortnight. The published journey, The Nile & the Red Sea, runs 13 days and adds two nights at the Mena House after the sea, from €7,999 per person (for two or more travellers, in luxury hotels, with domestic flights and the visa included); honeymoon versions are re-ordered and tailored to suit. If the river is the heart of it, The Complete Egypt gives five nights aboard a private dahabiya from €7,500 per person. FAQ

How many days does an Egypt honeymoon really need? Ten to twelve days lets you take Cairo, the river and the sea at honeymoon pace. With eight days or fewer, choose two of the three (Cairo and the river, or the river and the sea) rather than spend it packing. Four to six days works only as the river alone.

Is the boat private, or will other guests be aboard? It depends on the boat. The dahabiya on The Complete Egypt is private, with no one else aboard, which is the whole honeymoon case for it. The Oberoi Zahra on The Nile & the Red Sea is a cruiser of 27 to 28 cabins and suites, so you share the ship, though not your car or your Egyptologist.

We're marrying in summer: is Egypt too hot in June, July or August? For the temples, honestly, yes: Luxor and Aswan average about 41 °C by day in those months. Delay the journey to October, when the sea is still warm, or keep to the Red Sea and Cairo's museums and save the monuments for a second trip together.

What does a luxury Egypt honeymoon cost? Sillage's published journeys run from €2,190 to €11,650 per person, for two or more travellers in luxury hotels, with domestic flights and the visa included; Christmas and New Year on the Nile starts from €9,999. The two best suited are The Complete Egypt from €7,500 and The Nile & the Red Sea from €7,999 per person, before the tailoring that makes it yours. Peak periods carry a supplement, the enquiry is free, and the price is confirmed in writing before anything is booked.

Can we honeymoon in Egypt over Christmas or New Year? Yes. It is Egypt's finest-weather fortnight, and also its busiest and dearest. It works when booked nine to twelve months ahead; the detail, including Coptic Christmas on 7 January, is in our Christmas and New Year guide.

Is Egypt safe for two travellers on a honeymoon? A private journey adds structure: your own car and driver, your own certified Egyptologist, and a team reachable at any hour, in a country that received about 19 million visitors in 2025. Read your government's current travel advice before booking, and carry comprehensive insurance, which is a condition of booking with us.

Will we be travelling with other guests at any point? Not in your car or with your Egyptologist, and not on a private dahabiya. There are no scheduled departures and no shared groups. The exceptions are the places you would expect: other guests at your hotel, and on the Oberoi Zahra if your journey uses it.

The takeaway

Egypt is a fine luxury honeymoon when it is shaped like one: the stones in the morning, the river through the afternoon, and the sea to finish. Choose the boat first, because it decides the journey.
